newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr bruised vs yen in Tokyo, falls over one yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr bruised vs yen in Tokyo, falls over one yen.

text.p: 0651 GMT 2400 GMT NYK CLOSE
The dollar came under fresh attack from massive dollar sales against the yen in Tokyo on Thursday, with panic sales by trust banks pushing it down more than one yen to a four-month low of 115.60 yen.
Stop-loss sales and some exporter selling accelerated the dollar's slide and dealers in Tokyo were focusing on how far it might fall amid an absence of major buyers.

"There are more who must hurry to sell dollars. You can't predict how far the dollar will fall before examining the magnitude of their sales," said Koichi Kubo, assistant general manager of the forex group at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.
Dealers said buy-and-sell relationships in dollar/yen trading have reversed after the government's efforts to talk the dollar down to avoid friction with the United states.
"When you look around, it's very difficult to find buyers today," said a dealer at a European bank.
Among the major dollar sellers were Japanese trust banks acting on behalf of corporate pension funds.
Trust bank sources said there would be more dollar sales by the banks if the dollar kept falling.
A senior trader at a trust bank said pension funds were generally reluctant to wait for the dollar to rebound for their sales and perferred to dump dollars amid falls.
"What they are doing is to trying to avoid the worst case by fixing profits or losses," he added.
Sales by trust banks have exaggerated the speed of the dollar's falls and dealers said there was a risk of an even steeper drop if life insurance firms and exporters followed their move.
The European bank dealer said the dollar was likely in the near term to test 115.50 yen and 115.00 yen, where a large amount of stop-loss dollar sales orders are in place.
More large stop-loss orders are seen at 113 yen, and a break of that point would send the dollar down to 110 yen.
A chief dealer at another European bank in Tokyo said: "Since the dollar/yen fell through a 200-day moving average of 116.70 yen, it was likely to drift downward."
He said remarks by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka on Thursday were taken by the market to mean the Japanese government was not worried about the dollar's falls.
Mitsuzuka was quoted by Jiji news agency on Thursday as saying that the agreement on currencies by the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations has "sufficiently" filtered into the currency market.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, declined to elaborate on whether this meant that Japan did not wish for a further fall of the dollar.
He also declined to comment when asked whether the pace of the dollar's fall was too rapid and when asked what impact the dollar/yen rate would have on the Japanese economy.

A European bank dealer in Singapore said there was selling of dollars on behalf of regional investors around 116.20/30 yen. "This was also cutting of long positions. I see the market hasn't really turned short yet. The big long-term investors are not short yet so there's more to come," he said.
Some dealers said they were waiting for a speech by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin later on Thursday.

But analysts said that as long as U.S. financial markets were stable and inflation stayed under control, the United States would be happy with the dollar's falls. ---Singapore newsroom (65-8703080) --- Tatsuo Ito in Tokyo 81-3-3432-1396
